note: A general description of mechanical engineering roles. It is not a job description or hiring requirement from any company and is not used for measurement or scoring.

ROLE_DESIGN_V2.summary: Setting the shape, dimensions, materials and tolerances of a product or device, and releasing drawings and a bill of materials that can be built as they are
ROLE_DESIGN_V2.practiceWhere: in a machine design course project or your capstone design

TD01.why: Fixing shape, dimensions and tolerances is the core of a design role.
TD01.ctx: in a machine design course project or your capstone design

TD06.why: Choosing a material and grade for the loads and operating environment gives you the basis for the material field on the drawing.
TD06.ctx: in a design project where you have to pick the material yourself

out.J3: Note on why you chose the material

TD11.why: Deciding which of several competing requirements to protect first comes before any design work starts.
TD11.ctx: when you sort out the requirements for a team design project

J1.task: When you get a design brief, separate the functions the device must have from the ones you will not cover this time, and write both on the first page of your design specification.
J1.output: One page of design scope and exclusions
J1.check: Are the excluded functions listed together with the reason for leaving them out?

J2.task: Turn the requirements you received into design conditions such as loads, dimensions, operating environment and assembly constraints, and rank the ones that conflict.
J2.check: Does every condition have a number or a way to judge it?

J3.task: Pick one value yourself, such as a shaft diameter, a plate thickness or a fit tolerance grade, justify it from the loads and function, and keep the calculation.
J3.output: One section of a design calculation
J3.check: Can you explain the value you chose in terms of load or function?

J4.task: Work out the strength of a part or the life of a bearing two ways, by hand calculation and with a simple CAD analysis, and decide which result to base the design on.
J4.output: Note comparing the two calculation methods
J4.check: Where the two values differ, did you write the reason in one line?

J5.task: Put the assembly drawing, part drawings and bill of materials (BOM) together as one set that someone else could send straight out for machining.
J5.output: One set of assembly drawing, part drawings and BOM
J5.check: Are all dimensions, tolerances, materials and quantities on it?

J6.task: Calculate the tolerance stack-up between mating parts and check that they still assemble in the worst-case combination.
J6.check: Does it show the clearance or interference at the worst case?

J7.task: Pick one spot where a prototype did not fit or broke during assembly, narrow the cause down to dimensions, material or machining, and revise the drawing.
J7.output: Root cause note and drawing revision history
J7.check: Are the revision and the reason for it recorded in the drawing history?

J8.task: After a team design review, record whether your proposal was adopted and, if it was changed, which comments changed it.
J8.check: Does it say who accepted or changed the proposal, and on what grounds?

responsibilities: Designing the shape and dimensions of new and revised parts
Allocating tolerances and choosing fits
Selecting materials and standard parts (bearings, fasteners, gears and so on)
Producing assembly drawings, part drawings and BOMs, and managing design changes

process.what: Target performance, available space and a cost target arrive through a specification or a change request.
You sketch two or three concepts, compare their load paths and assembly order, and pick one.
You set thicknesses, sections, fastening, materials and tolerances, and record the reasoning in a design calculation.
With the analysis, manufacturing and quality engineers, you check for interference and how easy the part is to make.
The prototype is assembled and tested, and the measured values are compared with the drawing.
You release the final drawings and manage every later change through revisions.

knowledge: Mechanics of materials (stress, strain, buckling)
Machine element design (shafts, bearings, gears, fasteners)
Engineering drawing and geometric tolerancing
Engineering materials and basic heat treatment
tools: 3D CAD (SolidWorks, CATIA or NX, whichever your school uses)
2D drawings with GD&T callouts
Tolerance stack-up spreadsheet
National and ISO standards and standard-part catalogues
experiences: Drawing parts and assemblies yourself and sending them out to be made
Setting a dimension or tolerance with a calculation behind it
Revising a drawing because a prototype did not fit
entry: Take on the mechanism design and drawings in your capstone project
On a student competition team such as Formula Student or a robotics team, own one part from design through to manufacture
Take apart a mechanical product at home, redraw its parts, and work out how it is fastened and what it is made of

learnOrder.why: What a designer hands over is a drawing, and if you cannot read one you cannot fix anyone else's design either.

learnOrder.step: Hand calculations in mechanics and machine elements
learnOrder.why: You explain why a thickness or diameter is what it is through the calculation.
Whether parts assemble is often decided by the tolerances.
A drawing that checks out on paper but cannot be made comes straight back from the shop floor.

firstProject.title: Design one small mechanism from start to finish
firstProject.goal: Choose a mechanism such as a hand-cranked gear reducer or a small vice, and complete the assembly drawing, part drawings and design calculation as one set
steps: Write the required function, size and load conditions on one page
Size the shaft, bearings and bolts by hand calculation
Assemble it in 3D CAD and check interference and tolerance stack-up
Add tolerances and materials to the part drawings, then make one on a 3D printer or in the school workshop and assemble it
firstProject.output: A set of assembly and part drawings, a design calculation, and a record of the prototype build and revisions
firstProject.check: Can you justify every dimension and tolerance on the drawings?

portfolio: A set of assembly and part drawings with the BOM
A design calculation that sets a shaft diameter or wall thickness
One page on where you put the tight tolerances and why

interview.q: Have you set a dimension or tolerance yourself? What did you base the value on?
interview.why: Design means choosing values, and a designer is expected to explain the basis for each one.

interview.q: Before the parts were made, how did you check that they would assemble?
interview.why: Tolerance stack-up and interference checks are part of every drawing release.

interview.q: When a prototype did not fit or broke, what did you change?
interview.why: How you narrow the cause down to dimensions, material or machining shows your design judgement.

postingCheck: Whether the role works on mechanisms inside a product or on production machinery and equipment
Whether the posting names the CAD software you would use
Whether an engineering licence or certification is listed as a plus, where your country has one
ROLE_DESIGN_V2.watch: What a design engineer works on varies a lot from company to company. Two postings with the same title, such as Mechanical Design Engineer, can mean the mechanisms inside consumer electronics or the design of production equipment, and the tools and judgements differ. Look at the product line in the posting first and match the examples in your portfolio to it.

ROLE_CAE_V2.summary: Predicting strength, life, temperature and vibration by calculation before anything is built, and handing that prediction back to design along with the reasons to trust it
ROLE_CAE_V2.practiceWhere: in a finite element analysis course project or your capstone

TD02.why: Setting constraints, loads and material properties to predict strength and life is the core of an analysis role.
TD02.ctx: in a finite element analysis course project or your capstone

TD03.why: Setting thermal and flow boundary conditions to predict temperatures and pressure drop is how cooling performance gets judged.
TD03.ctx: in heat transfer or fluid mechanics projects

out.J2: Thermal and flow analysis conditions table
out.J6: Comparison of 1D calculation and simulation results

TD04.why: Predicting natural frequencies and mode shapes gives the evidence behind vibration and noise fixes.
TD04.ctx: in a vibration lab or a modal analysis project

out.J1: Note on the frequency range to study
out.J6: Table matching simulated and measured modes

J1.task: Before you start an analysis, write on one page which behaviour you will look at (static strength, fatigue, buckling and so on) and which features you will simplify away.
J1.output: Note on analysis scope and assumptions
J1.check: Are the removed features listed together with the reason for removing them?

J2.task: Pick the worst case from the project's operating conditions and turn it into analysis conditions such as loads, constraints and temperatures.
J2.check: Does every condition say where its value came from?

J3.task: Choose the constraint locations, load points and material properties yourself, and write one line on how the result would change if you had chosen differently.
J3.check: Can you explain how the constraint matches the real way the part is held?

J4.task: Run the model at three mesh sizes to see whether the result converges, and check its order of magnitude with a hand calculation such as beam theory.
J4.output: Mesh convergence table and one page of hand calculations
J4.check: Where the hand calculation and the simulation differ, did you explain why?

J5.task: Write up the conditions, assumptions, results and verdict in a report detailed enough for someone else to rebuild the same model.
J5.check: Could a reader reproduce your result from the report alone?

J6.task: Compare values measured in a mechanics or vibration lab with your simulation at the same location and under the same load.
J6.check: Did you compare at the same location and under the same conditions?

J7.task: When simulation and measurement disagree, check boundary conditions, then material properties, then the mesh, fix the model and run it again.
J7.check: Did you record what you changed and how much the gap closed?

J8.task: Record whether your results changed a thickness or shape in the team design, and if they did not, why not.
J8.output: Record of design changes from your analysis
J8.check: Does it say which dimension changed and which result it was based on?

responsibilities: Structural strength and fatigue life analysis and verdicts
Thermal and flow analysis to predict temperatures and pressure drop
Modal and vibration analysis and review of fixes
Correlating analysis with test results and standardising analysis procedures

process.what: Design asks questions such as whether this shape will hold or whether the temperature stays within the limit.
You take the load history, material, required life and allowable stress, and decide what to study and how far to simplify.
You simplify the geometry, set the boundary conditions and mesh, and run the analysis.
Mesh convergence, hand calculations and earlier analyses tell you whether the answer is believable.
You compare the result with the acceptance criteria and, if it falls short, propose the dimensions or shape to change.
When test results come in, you compare them with the analysis and update the model.

knowledge: Mechanics of materials and solid mechanics
Principles of the finite element method
Heat transfer and fluid mechanics
Basics of mechanical vibration and fatigue
tools: Finite element software (ANSYS, Abaqus or whatever your school uses)
Basic computational fluid dynamics
MATLAB or Python for post-processing and reporting
Material property data and handbooks of hand-calculation formulas
experiences: Setting analysis conditions yourself and making the pass or fail call
Comparing simulation results with lab measurements
Fixing a model and running it again after an odd result
entry: Extend a finite element course assignment into a report that checks the results against hand calculations
Take on the analysis in your capstone team and provide the evidence for design changes
Join a lab that combines simulation and testing as an undergraduate research assistant

learnOrder.step: Hand calculations in mechanics of materials
learnOrder.why: A hand calculation is your first check on whether a simulation result makes sense.

learnOrder.step: Finite element principles and boundary conditions
learnOrder.why: The same geometry can give very different results depending on how you constrain it.
Results without a convergence check are not accepted as a basis for design.
Once you have explained a gap between simulation and test, you can give reasons to trust your results.

firstProject.title: Analyse a bracket and check it against a test
firstProject.goal: Find the stress and deflection of a simple cantilever bracket three ways, by hand calculation, finite element analysis and measurement, and reconcile them
steps: Calculate deflection and peak stress by hand using beam theory
Model the same geometry in finite element software and check convergence over three mesh sizes
Load the bracket in the mechanics lab and measure deflection or strain
Put the three values in one table and write down why they differ
firstProject.output: An analysis report, a hand-calculation, simulation and measurement comparison table, and one page of conditions and assumptions
firstProject.check: Where the three values differ, can you say which one you trust and why?

portfolio: An analysis report covering conditions, assumptions and the verdict
A mesh convergence table with a hand-calculation check
A record of correlating analysis with test and revising the model

interview.q: How did you choose the constraints in your analysis? How would the result have changed if you had applied them differently?
interview.why: The same model can give very different results depending on the boundary conditions, and you need to be able to explain your choice.

interview.q: How did you confirm your analysis result was right?
interview.why: An analysis engineer does not stop at producing a number and is accountable for whether it holds up.

interview.q: When simulation and test disagreed, what did you suspect first?
interview.why: The order in which you narrow down causes shows how much analysis you have really done.

postingCheck: Whether the role covers structural, thermal-fluid or vibration analysis
Whether it is analysis only or design with analysis
Whether it asks for a master's degree or higher, and which software it names
ROLE_CAE_V2.watch: Dedicated analysis roles such as CAE Analyst or Simulation Engineer tend to sit in research centres and large development organisations, and many postings ask for a master's degree. If you are applying with a bachelor's degree, it is realistic to also look at design roles that include analysis work.

ROLE_RND_V2.summary: Taking on a technical problem that has no specification yet, and first working out what has to be achieved and how to approach it
ROLE_RND_V2.practiceWhere: as an undergraduate research assistant or in your final-year research project

TD06.why: When there is no method to use, you build and test a new combination of material and treatment, which is the classic case of advanced development creating a method.
TD06.ctx: as an undergraduate research assistant or in your final-year research project

out.J4: Note on why you chose the method
out.J7: Record of combinations that failed and why

TD05.why: When even the required motion has not been set, you narrow down what has to move and by how much.
TD05.ctx: in a capstone or competition where you design a new mechanism

out.J2: Table of must-have and dropped requirements

TD03.why: You set an assumption to test and check it first with a small experiment, an approach often used on topics such as thermal management.
TD03.ctx: in a thermal-fluids lab or your final-year research project

J1.task: When you get a vague goal such as make it lighter or make it quieter, narrow it to one problem you will solve this time and write it as a one-line question.
J1.output: One-line research question with a scope note
J1.check: Is the question written so an experiment or calculation can answer it?

J2.task: Split the requirements into those you must meet and those you will drop this time, and write why you dropped each one.
J2.check: Does every dropped requirement have a reason?

J3.task: Pick one of two or three candidate approaches and write down the assumptions that have to hold for it to work.
J3.output: Note on the chosen method and assumptions to test
J3.check: Did you identify the assumption most likely to fail first?

J4.task: Search papers and patents to see how others solved the same problem, summarise them, and note why you cannot use them as they are.
J4.check: Does it say how your approach differs from earlier ones?

J5.task: Keep a lab notebook of conditions, procedures and results so someone else could get the same result.
J5.check: Could another person run the same experiment from your notebook alone?

J6.task: Test one of your assumptions first with a small experiment or quick calculation, and decide whether it held.
J6.check: Did you write the pass criterion before you ran the check?

J7.task: Pick one attempt that did not work, write why, and decide whether to change direction or only change the conditions.
J7.output: Failure record and direction decision note
J7.check: Did you explain the failure with experimental results?

J8.task: Record how your results fed into the next experiment or the team's design direction.
J8.check: Does it say who picked up what from your results?

responsibilities: Concept review and feasibility checks for new structures and approaches
Prior art searches in papers and patents, and technology trend summaries
Building proof-of-concept prototypes and running experiments
Writing up specifications and methods to hand over to development

process.what: A future technology, or a problem current methods cannot solve, arrives as a project.
A prior art search filters out what is already known, and you decide the problem to solve and the requirements to drop.
You choose an approach and decide which assumption to test first.
You check the assumption with a quick prototype or a simple experiment.
Based on the result, you decide whether to continue, change the conditions or stop.
You write up what works, under which conditions, and what failed, so development can take it on.

knowledge: Core mechanics (solids, thermodynamics, fluids, dynamics)
Design of experiments and interpreting results
Engineering materials and basic manufacturing processes
How to read technical papers and patents
tools: Your library's paper databases and patent databases such as Google Patents or Espacenet
Lab notebooks and version control
MATLAB or Python for organising experimental data
Rapid prototyping tools such as 3D printers and laser cutters
experiences: Narrowing a vague topic down to a clear question
Setting an assumption and testing it by experiment
Recording a failed result and changing direction
entry: Join a lab as an undergraduate research assistant and take on one experiment in a lab project
When you choose a final-year research topic, do the prior art search yourself
Build a proof-of-concept prototype for a student design or invention competition

learnOrder.why: It is the first step to avoid solving a problem that is already solved.

learnOrder.step: Narrowing the problem and setting assumptions
learnOrder.why: Exploratory work never ends unless you set its scope.
A quick test of one assumption sets the direction sooner than a big prototype.
Methods that failed, and why, become the next person's starting point.

firstProject.title: Set one assumption and test it by experiment
firstProject.goal: Choose a topic you can test in your department's labs (heat sink fin shape, or print orientation and strength of 3D printed specimens, for example), set one assumption and settle it by experiment
steps: Narrow the topic to a one-line question and summarise three or four prior sources
Before the experiment, write down the assumption to test first and the pass criterion
Run a comparison experiment on small specimens or prototypes while varying the conditions
Decide from the results whether to continue or change direction, and record why on one page
firstProject.output: Research question and prior art table, lab notebook, and a one-page direction decision
firstProject.check: Could another person repeat the experiment from your notebook alone?

portfolio: One page showing how you narrowed the question
A table of assumptions and what the checks showed
A record of attempts that failed and why

interview.q: When you were given a vague topic, what did you decide first?
interview.why: Advanced development starts with narrowing down the problem yourself.

interview.q: When there was no set method, how did you choose one?
interview.why: Building the method yourself is what separates this role from Analysis and Prediction.

interview.q: When you realised partway through that something would not work, what did you do?
interview.why: Admitting quickly that something failed and changing direction happens often in this role.

postingCheck: Whether advanced development here is close to basic research or to pre-production development
Whether a master's or PhD is required
Whether the technical area (materials, thermal management, actuation and so on) matches your research experience
ROLE_RND_V2.watch: Advanced development and research roles often hire graduate degree holders. As an undergraduate, you can build research assistant experience while weighing graduate school, or start in a development role and move across later.

ROLE_TEST_V2.summary: Checking whether a prototype or product meets its requirements by setting the measurement method and acceptance criteria, measuring, and issuing the verdict in a test report
ROLE_TEST_V2.practiceWhere: in a mechanical engineering lab course or capstone performance testing

TD07.why: Choosing what to measure, the acceptance criteria and the fixtures, then making the call, is the core of a test role.
TD07.ctx: in a mechanical engineering lab course or capstone performance testing

TD04.why: Measuring vibration and sound and tracing where they come from is the work you do on noise and vibration testing.
TD04.ctx: in a vibration lab or a noise measurement project

out.J4: Note on measurement points and method

TD09.why: The condition of the equipment decides the result, so this is where you check calibration and equipment status before testing.
TD09.ctx: before taking measurements with lab equipment

J1.task: When you take on a test, separate what this test will and will not judge, and write it at the top of the test plan.
J1.output: One page of test purpose and scope
J1.check: Are what is judged and what is excluded clearly separated?

J2.task: Before testing, turn the requirements or standards into measured quantities, measurement methods and acceptance criteria.
J2.check: Are the acceptance criteria written as numbers before the test?

J3.task: Decide how to hold the specimen and where to apply the load, then build or choose a simple fixture.
J3.output: Fixture sketch and note on how the specimen is held
J3.check: Can you explain how the fixture matches real operating conditions?

J4.task: Measure the same quantity two ways (a strain gauge and a displacement sensor, for example) and decide which to use for the verdict.
J4.check: Did you write the limit of the method you chose in one line?

J5.task: Put the specimen, conditions, equipment, measurements and verdict into a one-page test report.
J5.check: Are specimen, conditions, equipment and verdict all included?

J6.task: Measure the same specimen several times, look at the scatter, and check whether it affects the verdict.
J6.output: Repeat measurement table with spread calculation
J6.check: Did you write how you will handle values close to the pass line?

J7.task: If a test gave unstable values, change the fixture, sensor, specimen and environment one at a time to find the cause, fix the method and measure again.
J7.check: Did you confirm the scatter dropped after the fix?

J8.task: Record how your verdicts changed the team's design or the next test plan.
J8.output: Record of how verdicts were used
J8.check: Does it say who used your test report for which decision?

responsibilities: Writing test plans and setting acceptance criteria
Designing test fixtures and setting up instrumentation
Running performance, durability and environmental tests and processing the data
Writing test reports and making the pass or fail call

process.what: Design or quality asks you to judge whether a prototype meets its requirements.
You read the standards and requirements and decide what to measure, how many, under which conditions, and where the pass line is.
You build fixtures, set up sensors and data acquisition, and check calibration status.
You run the test and use repeat measurements to see how much the values scatter.
You compare the results with the criteria, make the call and issue the test report.
If it fails, you send the results back to design and analysis and set the retest conditions.

knowledge: Measurement engineering and sensor principles
Mechanical engineering labs (materials, thermal-fluids, vibration)
Basic statistics (mean, standard deviation, measurement uncertainty)
Basics of mechanics of materials and vibration
tools: Data acquisition hardware and software such as LabVIEW
Sensors such as strain gauges, accelerometers and thermocouples
MATLAB, Python or Excel for processing measurement data
How to find test standards (ISO, ASTM and national standards)
experiences: Setting acceptance criteria before running a test
Mounting sensors yourself and taking measurements
Fixing a measurement method or fixture because the values were unstable
entry: In your lab reports, add the acceptance criteria and the spread of repeat measurements
Take on performance test planning and measurement in your capstone team
On a student vehicle or drone competition team, take charge of collecting driving or flight data

learnOrder.why: You can only trust a value if you know where error enters between the sensor and the record.
A single value is not enough for a verdict, and you have to look at the scatter too.
If you do not write the criteria first, you end up fitting the criteria to the results.
How you hold the specimen changes what you measure.

firstProject.title: Write one test from plan to report
firstProject.goal: Pick a capstone part or a 3D printed specimen and do the test plan, measurement, verdict and report in one go
steps: Before testing, write down what you will judge and the acceptance criteria
Decide how to hold the specimen and build a simple fixture
Measure several times under the same conditions and work out the mean and spread
Compare with the criteria, make the call, and write it up as a one-page test report
firstProject.output: Test plan, repeat measurement table and a one-page test report
firstProject.check: Were the acceptance criteria set before you saw the results?

portfolio: A test report that goes all the way to the verdict
A fixture sketch and test procedure
One page on the spread of repeat measurements and how you handled it

interview.q: Have you set acceptance criteria before a test? Where did they come from?
interview.why: Setting the criteria first is basic practice in test work.

interview.q: If you measured the same thing several times and got different values, how did you make the call?
interview.why: How you handle scatter shows how well you understand measurement.

interview.q: When a measurement looked wrong, what did you check first?
interview.why: Narrowing the cause through fixture, sensor, specimen and environment is the same order used in practice.

postingCheck: Whether you test parts or complete products, and whether it is durability, environmental or noise and vibration testing
Whether the role is hands-on with equipment or focused on analysing results
Whether you would work at a proving ground or in a test lab inside a plant
ROLE_TEST_V2.watch: Test and validation engineers often work in a research centre's test building or in a lab inside a plant, so check the location first. Postings also appear under titles such as Validation Engineer, Test Engineer or Reliability Test Engineer, so read the duties section rather than filtering by title.

ROLE_MFG_V2.summary: Choosing the processes, machining sequence, conditions and tooling so designed parts and products can be made again and again at the same quality
ROLE_MFG_V2.practiceWhere: in a manufacturing processes workshop or an industry internship

TD08.why: Setting processes, machining sequence and the range of process conditions is the core of manufacturing engineering.
TD08.ctx: in a manufacturing processes workshop or an industry internship

TD01.why: This is where you look at how easy a part is to make and ask design to change it, which you do when reviewing drawings before production.
TD01.ctx: when you hand capstone drawings over for machining

TD09.why: Deciding what a machine will make and under which conditions requires knowing its specifications and capability.
TD09.ctx: when you use the machine tools in the workshop

J1.task: When you get a part to make, separate what you will decide (process, sequence, conditions) from what goes back to design (dimension changes and so on), and write it at the top of the process plan.
J1.check: Are the issues for design and the issues for you clearly separated?

J2.task: From the drawing tolerances and the required quantity, work out which processes and machine conditions can hold them.
J2.check: Is every tolerance paired with the process that will hold it?

J3.task: Decide the process and machining sequence for one part yourself, and write one line on why you rejected each alternative sequence.
J3.output: Process chart and sequence decision note
J3.check: Can you explain which surface you used as the datum and why?

J4.task: Run trial cuts at two or three levels of a condition such as cutting speed or feed, and find the range that gives the dimensions and surface finish you need.
J4.check: Does each condition have its dimensional or surface roughness result?

J5.task: Write the sequence and conditions as a work instruction that someone seeing it for the first time could follow.
J5.check: Could another student make the same part from your instruction alone?

J6.task: Measure several machined parts, compare them with the drawing tolerances, and calculate a process capability index.
J6.output: Dimensional measurement table and capability calculation
J6.check: Did you measure all parts with the same gauge and method?

J7.task: Pick one defective part, narrow the cause down to machine, material, conditions or operator method, and change the conditions or tooling.
J7.output: Defect cause and corrective action record
J7.check: Did you check whether the same defect came back after the fix?

J8.task: Record whether the conditions or work instruction you set were used as they are by your team or the workshop.
J8.output: Record of how the standard was applied
J8.check: Does it say who used the standard for which job?

responsibilities: Process design for new products and preparing the hand-over to production
Setting and standardising machining, forming and assembly conditions
Specifying tooling, jigs and fixtures, and equipment
Reducing defects and cycle time, and managing process data

process.what: Finished drawings and production volume targets come over from design.
You set the processes, sequence and inspection points, and choose the equipment and tooling needed.
In trial production you vary the conditions to find the range that works.
You turn the chosen conditions into work instructions and condition sheets for the shop floor.
You compare the defect rate and cycle time of early production with the targets.
When defects appear or targets are missed, you narrow down the cause and adjust conditions and tooling.

knowledge: Manufacturing processes (machining, forming, welding, assembly)
Engineering drawing and tolerances
Basic quality control (process capability, control charts)
Basic production management
tools: Basic CNC machining and CAM
Gauges such as vernier calipers, micrometers and height gauges
Basic design of experiments
Excel for organising process data
experiences: Machining parts yourself on machine tools
Varying conditions to find the range that works
Writing down a work sequence and handing it to someone else
entry: In your manufacturing workshop, set the machining sequence and conditions yourself and record them
Take on one process improvement project during an internship at a manufacturer
On a student competition team, take charge of machining and assembly order for the parts

learnOrder.why: Which surface you use as the datum sets the machining sequence and the accuracy.
You can only judge whether the conditions worked if you can read and measure tolerances.
Knowing the range that works, not a single point, keeps production stable.
Conditions are only followed if operators on the floor can follow what you wrote.

firstProject.title: Write the production readiness documents for one part
firstProject.goal: Pick a part made in your workshop, prepare a process chart, condition sheet and work instruction, then make several and check they fall within tolerance
steps: Read the drawing, choose the process and machining sequence, and draw a process chart
Do trial machining at two or three conditions and measure dimensions and surface finish
Make several of the same part at the chosen conditions and look at the dimensional spread
Write a work instruction and have another student follow it
firstProject.output: A process chart, condition trial record and work instruction
firstProject.check: When someone else follows the instruction, are their parts within tolerance?

portfolio: A work instruction and process chart
A trial record that sets the working range of conditions
A tooling sketch or a before and after comparison

interview.q: Have you set a machining sequence yourself? Why that order?
interview.why: Choosing the sequence and datums is where manufacturing engineering starts.

interview.q: How did you set the machining conditions? Did you keep the first ones you chose?
interview.why: How you find the working range shows your feel for the shop floor.

interview.q: When defects appeared, how did you narrow down the cause?
interview.why: Separating machine, material, conditions and method is something you do every day in this job.

postingCheck: Which process you would own: machining, assembly, welding or injection moulding
Whether the focus is launching new products or improving existing lines
The location, whether there is shift work, and whether a manufacturing or quality certification is listed as a plus
ROLE_MFG_V2.watch: Manufacturing engineers work at the plant, so the job is wherever the plant is. Postings with the same title, such as Manufacturing Engineer or Process Engineer, overlap with equipment roles to different degrees at each company, so read the duties section carefully.

ROLE_MAINT_V2.summary: Setting inspection, calibration and replacement criteria so production machinery and equipment keep performing, and finding the cause and bringing them back when they stop
ROLE_MAINT_V2.practiceWhere: while looking after lab equipment or during an industry internship

TD09.why: Setting inspection items, intervals and replacement criteria, and restoring stopped equipment, is the core of a maintenance role.
TD09.ctx: while looking after lab equipment or during an industry internship

TD08.why: Process conditions only hold if the equipment runs, so when deciding which machine to service first you look at the flow of the production line too.
TD08.ctx: when you observe a production line during an internship

out.J1: Note on the impact of equipment downtime

TD04.why: Reading the condition of rotating machinery from vibration and sound lets you catch a problem before it stops.
TD04.ctx: in a vibration measurement lab or when working with rotating equipment

J1.task: Pick a piece of equipment your lab or club uses often, write what gets blocked if it stops or drifts, and set the scope you will look after.
J1.output: Note on equipment and scope covered
J1.check: Does it list the equipment you will not cover and why?

J2.task: Read the equipment specifications and manual and turn the conditions to maintain (lubrication, temperature, accuracy and so on) into inspection items.
J2.check: Does every item have its normal range?

J3.task: Set an interval and replacement criterion for each inspection item yourself, and write the reason for each interval next to it.
J3.check: Can you explain why you made an interval shorter or longer?

J4.task: Check the equipment's sound, heat and vibration with instruments or by hand, record the normal state, and decide how you will spot warning signs.
J4.check: Is the line between normal and abnormal written down?

J5.task: Write up one breakdown or repair so that someone else could follow it in the same situation.
J5.check: Are symptom, cause, action and confirmation written in order?

J6.task: Check measuring equipment against a calibration reference or standard sample, and if there are several of the same unit, compare their readings.
J6.check: Did you record the difference from the reference and decide whether to keep using it?

J7.task: If a machine has shown the same symptom more than once, work out whether the machine, the operating conditions or the way it is used is to blame, and decide how to prevent it recurring.
J7.check: Do you have evidence that narrows it to one cause?

J8.task: Hand the operating method and inspection checklist to a junior student or teammate, and check that they keep using it after the hand-over.
J8.check: Could the person who took over do the inspection on their own?

responsibilities: Setting equipment inspection criteria and planning preventive maintenance
Analysing failure causes and repairing or modifying equipment
Managing spare parts and consumables
Keeping equipment history and reducing downtime

process.what: The floor reports that a machine has stopped, drifted or started to sound different.
You try to reproduce the symptom and look at sound, heat, vibration and the machine's history.
You rule out candidate causes in the machine, the conditions and the way it is used, one by one.
You replace or adjust parts and modify the equipment if needed.
After the fix you check performance and record the failure and what was done.
To stop the same failure coming back, you revise inspection items, intervals and spare part levels.

knowledge: Machine elements (bearings, gears, belts, seals) and lubrication
Hydraulics, pneumatics and basic electrical and control (PLC concepts)
Basic mechanical vibration
Basics of wear and fatigue
tools: Vibration meters and infrared thermometers
Inspection checklists and equipment history records (Excel or a maintenance management system)
Reading hydraulic, pneumatic and electrical schematics
Basic hand tools and shaft alignment
experiences: Taking equipment apart and putting it back together
Finding a failure cause by ruling out possibilities one by one
Writing an inspection checklist or operating guide and handing it on
entry: Make an inspection checklist for one machine in your department's lab or workshop and take charge of it
During an internship at a manufacturer, shadow the maintenance team and keep notes
Take hydraulics, pneumatics or PLC lab courses and build circuits yourself

learnOrder.why: Equipment failures often start in machine elements such as bearings, gears and seals.
If you only look at the mechanical side, you miss failures that come from air or electrical systems.

learnOrder.step: Reading condition from sound, heat and vibration
learnOrder.why: Catching warning signs early lets you fix equipment before it stops.
With records built up, you can change intervals and replacement criteria with evidence.

firstProject.title: Build a maintenance log for one piece of lab equipment
firstProject.goal: Pick a machine your department uses often and create an inspection checklist, a normal condition record and a breakdown response procedure as one set
steps: Read the manual and specifications and write the inspection items and normal ranges
For a month, inspect at the interval you set and record sound, temperature and vibration
Ask the lab technician or teaching assistant about past breakdowns or problems and write up causes and actions
Hand the checklist and procedure to a junior student and have them do an inspection on their own
firstProject.output: Inspection checklist, condition record and a one-page breakdown response procedure
firstProject.check: Can the person taking over do an inspection and the first response from the procedure alone?

portfolio: An inspection checklist with items and intervals
A record of failure symptoms, causes and actions
A calibration check sheet or hand-over document

interview.q: Have you set an inspection interval? Why that interval?
interview.why: Setting inspection criteria with evidence behind them is central to maintenance work.

interview.q: How did you notice the equipment was not right?
interview.why: How you read the warning signs shows how well you understand the machine.

interview.q: When the same failure happened again, what did you change?
interview.why: Judgement that prevents recurrence lasts longer than a single repair.

postingCheck: Whether you would handle mechanical maintenance only, or electrical and controls maintenance as well
Whether there is shift work or on-call duty
Whether a maintenance, mechanical or HVAC licence or certification is listed as a plus, where your country has one
ROLE_MAINT_V2.watch: Equipment and maintenance roles are based on the plant floor or at a plant site, and can involve shift work or on-call duty. In equipment-heavy industries the same work is often advertised as Equipment Engineer or Maintenance Engineer, so search with a wide range of titles.

ROLE_QUALITY_V2.summary: Assuring through control criteria and verdicts that production keeps meeting requirements and standards, and confirming through life testing that products do not fail during their service life
ROLE_QUALITY_V2.practiceWhere: in a quality control or engineering statistics course project or an industry internship

TD10.why: Deciding which characteristics to control, their limits and acceptance criteria, and assuring production quality and life, is the core of a quality role.
TD10.ctx: in a quality control or engineering statistics course project or an industry internship

TD07.why: Confirming first that the measurement is trustworthy is what lets you turn verdicts into a standard for all of production.
TD07.ctx: when you handle measurement data in a mechanical engineering lab

TD08.why: Checking whether the set process conditions are being kept is how you find out why a defect occurred.
TD08.ctx: when you look at process data during an internship

J1.task: Pick a product, work out the most dangerous failure under the customer's conditions of use, and choose the characteristics to control.
J1.check: Is the reason for each characteristic tied to how the customer uses the product?

J2.task: Turn drawing tolerances and customer requirements into inspection items, sample sizes and acceptance criteria.
J2.check: Does every item have a measurement method and an acceptance criterion?

J3.task: Build a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), rate severity and occurrence for each failure mode, and decide yourself which items to address first.
J3.check: Can you explain how you chose the items to address first?

J4.task: Draw a control chart from dimensional data you collected in a lab or project, and calculate a process capability index.
J4.check: Did the data come from the same conditions and the same measurement method?

J5.task: Write up the cause, countermeasure and verification of one defect as a corrective action report in a format such as 8D.
J5.check: Does it include the verification results after the countermeasure was applied?

J6.task: Collect times to failure from repeat or accelerated tests, estimate the life distribution, and compare it with the target life.
J6.check: Did you note how the test conditions differ from real use?

J7.task: Pick a case where the same defect came back, and set separate countermeasures for why it occurred and why it was not caught.
J7.check: Are the two countermeasures written separately?

J8.task: Record whether the criteria or countermeasures you set changed an inspection method or a process.
J8.check: Does it say which process or inspection changed and how?

responsibilities: Setting inspection standards and control plans
Analysing process quality data and running control charts
Analysing defect causes and corrective action
Planning reliability tests, assessing life and handling customer quality issues

process.what: You read the drawings and customer requirements and decide the characteristics to control and the inspection criteria.
Control charts and capability figures show whether production is staying within the criteria.
When a defect or customer complaint comes in, you quarantine the affected product and look for the cause.
You set separate countermeasures for occurrence and escape, then check they work.
Reliability tests show whether the product survives its intended service life.
You report the corrective action and revise the inspection standard and control plan.

knowledge: Quality control and engineering statistics (control charts, process capability, acceptance sampling)
Basic reliability engineering (life distributions, accelerated testing)
Measurement and tolerances
The basic framework of a quality management system (ISO 9001)
tools: Statistics software such as Excel or Minitab
FMEA, 8D and control plan templates
Measurement system analysis (repeatability and reproducibility)
Basic Weibull analysis
experiences: Drawing a control chart from measured data
Finding a defect cause, setting a countermeasure and checking it worked
Setting inspection criteria yourself
entry: Do your quality control or engineering statistics assignments with data you actually measured
During an internship at a manufacturer, take on one defect analysis with the quality team
Build an FMEA for your capstone result and include it in your presentation

learnOrder.why: Whether a process is within its criteria is judged from the spread of the data.
If the measurement wobbles, you reject good parts and pass bad ones.
Recording causes and countermeasures in a set format is the basic language of quality work.
A product that passed at shipment can still fail in use, so you have to look at life as well.

firstProject.title: Write a small quality report on one workshop part
firstProject.goal: Use dimensional data from several parts made in your workshop to build a control chart, a capability calculation and an FMEA, and propose one improvement
steps: Choose two or three control characteristics for one part and write the inspection criteria
Measure several parts with the same method, draw a control chart and calculate the capability index
List candidate causes of out-of-limit values or defects in an FMEA table
Write one countermeasure that separates occurrence and escape, and decide how you will check it worked
firstProject.output: Inspection criteria, control chart and capability calculation, FMEA table and a one-page countermeasure
firstProject.check: Is the criterion for judging whether the countermeasure worked written as a number?

portfolio: A control plan with control characteristics and inspection criteria
A corrective action report covering cause, countermeasure and verification
One page showing a life or process capability calculation

interview.q: When you chose what to control, what did you look at first?
interview.why: Quality starts with choosing what to control.

interview.q: How did you confirm that a countermeasure worked?
interview.why: A countermeasure without verification results is not accepted in a quality report.

interview.q: When the same problem came back, how did you respond?
interview.why: Looking at occurrence and escape separately is a basic skill in this role.

postingCheck: Whether the job is process quality, outgoing quality, supplier quality or reliability
Whether it includes handling customer quality requirements or quality audits
Whether a quality engineering certification or experience with a quality management system such as ISO 9001 or IATF 16949 is listed as a plus
ROLE_QUALITY_V2.watch: Quality roles are often split between the plant quality team and the reliability team at a research centre. The plant side involves frequent floor issues and customer contact, while the research side centres on testing and life analysis, so first check which side the posting is on. Titles you will see include Quality Engineer, Supplier Quality Engineer and Reliability Engineer.

ROLE_PM_V2.summary: On a development project that involves many people and departments, organising the requirements and setting roles, schedules and the scope of changes so the work fits together
ROLE_PM_V2.practiceWhere: as a capstone team lead or running a student competition team

TD11.why: Breaking down requirements and setting acceptance criteria, schedules and interfaces is the core of technical planning.
TD11.ctx: as a capstone team lead or running a student competition team

TD12.why: Keeping records and versions so requirements and decisions can be traced later is how you manage a project's history.
TD12.ctx: when you manage team documents and change history

out.J5: Note on how change history is managed
out.J8: Example of the records being used

TD10.why: Deciding who meets which criteria and when is how you build test and verification stages into a development schedule.
TD10.ctx: when you add test and verification stages to a development schedule

J1.task: At the start of a team project, agree with your teammates what counts as done and what is out of scope, and write it on one page.
J1.check: Did every teammate agree to what is out of scope?

J2.task: Collect the requirements from your supervisor, teammates and the competition rules in one table, and add an acceptance criterion to each.
J2.check: Does every requirement have a way to verify it, and are conflicting requirements marked?

J3.task: Set the dimensions, signals and schedule that parts or subsystems must agree on, and decide who owns each one.
J3.check: Does every interface have a single owner?

J4.task: When a requirement changes, identify the parts and schedule items it affects and replan.
J4.check: Did a teammate check that you caught every affected item?

J5.task: Keep the requirements table, schedule and change history in one document the whole team works from.
J5.output: Requirements table, schedule and change history
J5.check: Can you trace who changed what and when?

J6.task: At the end of the project, go through the requirements table item by item and pick out anything not met.
J6.check: Does every unmet item have a reason?

J7.task: Pick one stage that slipped, narrow down why, and write how you will plan differently on the next project.
J7.output: Schedule slip cause and improvement note
J7.check: Do you have evidence that narrows it to one cause?

J8.task: Record whether the team actually worked to the schedule and task split you set, and what changed along the way.
J8.check: Does it say when and how the team used that schedule?

responsibilities: Organising requirements and finalising specifications for development projects
Planning schedule, staffing and budget, and tracking progress
Coordinating interfaces and design changes between departments
Running stage-gate reviews and reporting on the project

process.what: A new product development or an internal or publicly funded project is approved, with goals and a deadline.
You gather customer, regulatory and internal requirements into a requirements table with acceptance criteria.
You split the requirements by part and subsystem and set roles and interfaces.
You put design, prototype, test and production hand-over stages and review points on the schedule.
You check progress and, when requirements change, map the impact and revise the schedule.
You use the requirements table to confirm what was met, wrap up the project and pass it to the next stage.

knowledge: Basic systems engineering (requirements, interfaces)
Product development stages and design reviews
Basic project management (schedule, resources, risk)
Engineering economics and cost basics
tools: Gantt charts and scheduling tools
A spreadsheet requirements traceability table
Shared documents and version control
Templates for meeting minutes and review records
experiences: Organising the requirements and schedule for a team project
Splitting roles and coordinating where the pieces meet
Replanning a schedule after the requirements changed
entry: Take on team lead, scheduling or documentation in your capstone
On a student vehicle or robotics competition team, handle interpreting the rules and managing the schedule
Help write project reports on an industry-sponsored project or during an internship

learnOrder.why: Once the requirements are laid out in a table, you can see which ones conflict.
Without a criterion for done, a project never finishes.
Problems during development often appear where parts meet parts and people meet people.
Requirements always change during development, and mapping the impact at that point is what keeps the schedule.

firstProject.title: Build a requirements table and schedule for your capstone
firstProject.goal: Organise one team project's requirements in a table, and manage acceptance criteria, roles, schedule and change history through to the end
steps: Gather the requirements from your supervisor, teammates and the rules in one table and add acceptance criteria
Break the requirements down by part and assign owners and interfaces
Put the design, build and test stages on the schedule and record progress every week
At the end, check compliance against the requirements table and write the reason for any item not met
firstProject.output: Requirements table, roles and interfaces table, schedule and change history
firstProject.check: At the end, can you answer from the table whether each requirement was met?

portfolio: A requirements table with acceptance criteria
A schedule and change history
One page setting out roles and interfaces

interview.q: Did requirements ever conflict on a team project? How did you sort them out?
interview.why: Laying conflicting requirements out in a table is where technical planning starts.

interview.q: When the requirements changed partway through, how did you revise the schedule?
interview.why: Mapping the impact of a change is the judgement used most often in project management.

interview.q: At the end of the project, how did you check that nothing was missing?
interview.why: Closing out against the requirements table is a basic habit in project management.

postingCheck: Whether technical planning here means running development projects or technology strategy and trend research
Whether it includes writing proposals and reports for publicly funded projects
Whether it hires graduates or asks for development experience
ROLE_PM_V2.watch: Technical planning and project management roles are often filled by people moving across from development, so there are few graduate openings. As a graduate, it is realistic to start in a design or test role, such as Mechanical Design Engineer or Test Engineer, and build project management experience from there.
